title: The Tilted and the Windy: Uranus and Neptune
objective: After this level you can describe Uranus’s sideways tilt and Neptune’s supersonic winds.
summary: Uranus rolls on its side with 42-year polar days; Neptune has the fastest winds known. Methane makes both of them blue.

cards.headline: On Uranus, a single day at the pole can last 42 years.
cards.body: Uranus and Neptune, the two ice giants, are the oddballs of the family. One rolls around the Sun on its side. The other has the fastest winds in the solar system.

cards.headline: A planet on its side
cards.body: Back in Level 5, Earth's lean of about 23.5° was enough to give you summer and winter. Uranus is tilted about 98°, so it essentially rolls around the Sun on its side. That makes for extreme seasons: each pole gets about 42 years of continuous sunlight, followed by 42 years of darkness. Be born at the start of a polar summer, and you'd be middle-aged by sunset.

cards.headline: The windiest planet
cards.body: Neptune has the fastest winds in the solar system, over 2,000 km/h. It's also so far out that one trip around the Sun takes about 165 years, which means it only finished its first full orbit since its discovery in 2011. And visitors are rare: Voyager 2 is the only spacecraft ever to drop by. Windy, remote, and hardly anyone calls.

cards.fact: Methane makes Uranus and Neptune blue.
cards.context: Methane in their atmospheres absorbs red light. Take the red out of sunlight, and what bounces back to your eye looks blue. Two very different oddballs, painted with the same trick.

cards.headline: Ice giants: visited
learned: Uranus is tilted about 98°, on its side
Its poles get 42-year days and nights
Neptune has the fastest winds: over 2,000 km/h

questions.prompt: Which planet has the fastest winds in the solar system?

options.label: Jupiter, with its Great Red Spot
options.rationale: Jupiter’s storms are huge, but Neptune’s winds are faster.

options.label: Uranus, the tilted planet
options.rationale: Uranus is known for its tilt.

options.label: Venus, with its thick air
options.rationale: Venus’s air is dense but its surface winds are slow.

questions.explanation: Neptune’s winds exceed 2,000 km/h, the fastest in the solar system.

questions.prompt: What gives Uranus and Neptune their blue color?

options.label: Methane in their atmospheres absorbing red light
Oceans of liquid water on their surfaces
Reflections of the blue sky of Earth
Ice crystals in their ring systems
options.rationale: Their color comes from their atmospheres.

questions.explanation: Methane absorbs red light, so the light these planets reflect looks blue.

questions.prompt: From Level 5: Earth’s 23.5° tilt gives us seasons. What does Uranus’s ~98° tilt do?

options.label: It cancels out seasons completely
options.rationale: A big tilt makes seasons more extreme, not absent.

options.label: It makes its seasons shorter than Earth’s
It gives extreme seasons, with 42-year polar days
It makes Uranus spin backwards like Venus
options.rationale: The tilt is about its axis, not the spin direction story.

questions.explanation: Uranus is tipped almost on its side, so each pole faces the Sun for about 42 years, then away for 42.
